text: For nearly four years I led UX design at PaySika, from the MVP to a multi-product neobank serving thousands of people across Central Africa. I owned the experience end to end — mobile, web, back office and the physical card — and measured my work the way the business did: in retention, in support tickets, and in the minutes a customer spends at a relay point.
heading: From first tap to daily habit

cards.title: Design team lead
cards.text: Took design from a solo effort to a small team, working shoulder to shoulder with product, engineering, compliance, operations and support.

cards.title: End-to-end, beyond the app
cards.text: Owned onboarding, KYC, transactions and card management, then the service around the card: ordering, home delivery, relay-point pickup and activation.

cards.title: Measured in outcomes
cards.text: A redesigned journey that lifted retention 40%, cut support tickets 60%, and took relay-point handover from 30 minutes to 10.

text: KYC was the biggest leak. The photo step failed quietly on most Android browsers in Cameroon, and drop-off clustered exactly where the product asked for trust without giving any back. The fix was less about visuals than honesty on every screen: what it costs, why we need it, what just happened. The card told a different story: once a customer ordered one, the journey left the app entirely — a courier, a relay point, a paper form — and nobody had mapped that half of the experience.
heading: Where the funnel was leaking

eyebrow: The other half of the journey
heading: The card was a service, not an object
text: Ordering a card was the easy part. What came next happened outside the product: an agent drove it across the city, a relay point held it, a customer queued for it, and someone in the office typed the delivery status in later. Designing that meant designing three things as one journey — the agent's step, the customer's wait, and the back-office handover — not decorating the screen where it all started.

cards.title: 30 minutes → 10
cards.text: The average time a customer spent between arriving at a relay point and leaving it, once paper forms and manual signatures became QR-code validation.

cards.title: 15 delivery agents
cards.text: Across Douala and Yaoundé, receiving orders and confirming handovers in an internal app I designed.

cards.title: Two markets
cards.text: Cameroon and Gabon, one product: the same card and app experience, with KYC rebuilt per market.

heading: Order, deliver, hand over, activate
text: Four touchpoints in one experience, and three of them happen away from a screen.

items.title: Ordering
items.description: Where the customer decides, with delivery method, fees and timing stated on the same screen.

items.title: Home delivery
items.description: The agent's route, with the customer's details and the handover confirmed in the app.

items.title: Relay-point pickup
items.description: QR-code validation replaced the paperwork, so the handover is recorded the moment it happens.

items.title: Activation
items.description: Back in the app, the card goes live, and the customer's first transaction tells us whether the journey worked.

items.title: The card itself
items.description: Production files and the mailer, designed so the first thing the customer sees is the card they waited for.

heading: The app our agents used
text: The delivery agents were not part of the product team, so the app had to be obvious on a phone in the middle of a shift: the order, the customer, the address, one button to confirm.

heading: One product, two sets of rules
text: When PaySika opened in Gabon, KYC in Cameroon was not KYC in Gabon: different documents, different checks, different expectations from the partner bank. I led the design across the mobile app and the back office so we kept one product with market-specific onboarding, rather than two apps that drift apart — and so the card journey behaved the same way in both.
The systems behind the shipped interface: documentation, requirements, mobile flows, physical-card production files, and the usability-testing archive.

items.title: Design system and team process
items.description: The UI standards, collaboration rituals, and the repeatable delivery pipeline I built so design kept pace with engineering.

items.title: Product requirements
items.description: Requirement docs connecting the dashboard, branding, KYC, fees, and mobile flows to clear, testable outcomes.

items.title: Mobile flows and product assets
items.description: The screens themselves: onboarding, transaction history, secure card flows, animations, and app assets.

items.title: Physical card and mailer
items.description: Production files for the physical Visa-partner card and its unboxing: packaging, print, envelope, and manufacturing specs.

items.title: Usability-testing archive
items.description: The consent forms, scripts, observer guides, reports, and recordings from the sessions that drove the redesign.

heading: The work behind the screens

text: Usability calls were product's; making sure what shipped still looked and felt like one product was mine, checked screen by screen so nothing drifted between Figma and production.

items.title: One design system
items.description: Tokens, components, and text styles in Figma, the single source every PaySika surface builds from.

items.title: Card state library
items.description: Every physical and virtual card state, active, locked, expired, inactive, designed once and reused everywhere a card appears.

items.title: Icon library
items.description: A shared icon set for card settings, mobile-money and bank partners, and card actions, so icons read the same on every screen.

items.title: Illustration library
items.description: Reusable illustrations for onboarding, KYC, empty states, and success moments, giving the product one consistent voice.

heading: One design system, every surface

text: A calm confirmation and a scary error state are doing different jobs, but they leave the user with the same question answered: is my money safe here? I designed to answer yes every time, and the retention and support-ticket numbers followed.
heading: Trust is designed one screen at a time

text: Product design at PaySika also meant being dependable inside the team: clarifying flows, unblocking teammates, and getting my hands dirty on things outside my lane. That's the startup spirit, turning messy product questions into decisions people can act on.
